one_liner: Ahead-of-time transpiler from type-annotated Python to C or Fortran extension modules; 5x-2000x faster than CPython on scalar-loop numeric kernels.
what_it_does: Pyccel translates a statically typed subset of Python (scalar type hints plus string hints such as 'float[:,:]' for NumPy arrays) into readable C or Fortran. It then compiles that code with a Python C wrapper into a module.<tag>.so that shadows the original .py on import. You call it as `pyccel compile mod.py --language c|fortran` or as `epyccel(func)` inside a session. Calling code does not change, but the translated module has to stay inside the supported subset: a variable keeps one type for its whole scope, and NumPy and SciPy calls are only partly covered.
how_it_is_fast: Pyccel does static type inference over the annotated code and emits plain loops over int64_t and double values and over NumPy-layout arrays (STC cspan in C, allocatable arrays in Fortran). The result has no interpreter dispatch, no boxing and no reference counting, and gcc, gfortran, icx or ifx then optimise it. Non-literal negative indexing gets no runtime check unless you request one, so array accesses compile to direct loads. OpenMP pragmas written as `#$ omp` comments and MPI give parallelism beyond what one core can do.
when_to_use: Pure-Python numeric loops (ODE integrators, stencils, graph shortest paths, recursion) that run 100x-1000x slower in CPython than in compiled code.
You want the generated C or Fortran to be readable and kept, for example to hand a kernel to an HPC code base or to read what the compiler sees.
Fortran-heavy scientific groups: in the published tables the Fortran backend is the steadier of the two (geomean about 383x over CPython in both the dev and 2.2.3 tables).
Shared-memory or MPI parallel kernels written in Python syntax, using `#$ omp` pragmas.
when_not_to_use: Code that already spends its time inside NumPy calls: FD Laplace, written with NumPy slices, gains only 4.8x with the C backend (729 ms vs 151 ms) because CPython was not the bottleneck.
Dynamic Python (types that change at run time, heterogeneous containers, arbitrary third-party libraries). Lists and tuples are only partly supported, and module-level tuples are not handled.
You need the fastest accelerator in this class: Pythran beats Pyccel's GNU C backend on 6 of 12 shared kernels (Dijkstra, M-D, the four FD solvers) in Pyccel's own table.
Windows deployments that use external libraries (support is documented as experimental and limited), or environments without a C or Fortran toolchain at build time.
Code that relies on Python's arbitrary-precision int: `int` becomes int64_t or integer(i64).

integration.dependencies: Python >=3.10, numpy>=2.1, sympy, textx, meson, ninja and a few small packages (PyPI 2.2.3); a C and/or Fortran compiler (GNU, Intel icx/ifx, LLVM clang/flang, NVIDIA nvc/nvfort); BLAS/LAPACK for linear algebra; optional OpenMP and MPI
integration.min_toolchain: Python 3.10; any supported C99/Fortran compiler family (versions not documented)
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS (CI for both, plus Intel and Anaconda jobs); Windows experimental
integration.thread_safety: not documented; generated modules can use OpenMP threads internally
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the compiled .so replaces the .py module with no change for callers, but the source must be annotated and stay within Pyccel's typed subset

gotchas: The headline table comes from an unreleased devel commit (0ccf9ec), timed as timeit best-of. The released PyPI 2.2.3 tables (pyperf mean) show a much slower GNU C backend: Euler 21.0 ms vs 6.94, Midpoint Explicit 42.2 vs 12.9, Midpoint Fixed 180 vs 47.4, FD L Convection 4.44 vs 2.04, M-D 106 vs 74.5. Its C-backend geomean over CPython 3.12 is about 210x, not 336x (derived from page data).

Harness flaw: the Midpoint Fixed kernel's derivative (humps_deriv) depends only on x, so its 10 'implicit' iterations per step all compute the same value. In the dev table Intel C runs it in 7.24 ms, exactly its Euler time and 6.5x faster than GNU C, which suggests the compiler collapsed the loop. The harness also never checks outputs across tools, even with -ffast-math and a tolerance-terminated Laplace loop whose iteration count can differ.
Indexing an array with a negative variable or expression is unchecked unless the function carries @allow_negative_index; the docs warn this 'can cause a crash'.
Open bug reports include memory leaks (#2435 in classes for C, #2342 with LLVM compilers), wrong numpy.sum translation of np.full arguments (#1815), and `and`/`or` translation problems (#2088).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Pyccel over Pythran when you want a Fortran backend or readable C/Fortran output with OpenMP/MPI pragmas; Pythran is as fast or faster on NumPy-style stencils and graph kernels in the same harness. Pick it over Cython, Shed Skin or Codon when the code is already numeric Python with type hints and you want no new syntax and no new runtime; pick those for general-purpose Python.
verified_claims_summary: Pyccel's own pyccel-benchmarks workflow ran 13 scalar-loop kernels under CPython 3.12 on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner (CPU unstated) with -O3 -march=native -ffast-math. Times are python3 -m timeit best-of in ms, compilation excluded. The devel GNU C backend was 4.8x (FD Laplace) to 1624x (FD Poisson) faster than CPython, geomean about 336x; the Fortran backend's geomean was about 388x. Pythran (geomean about 264x) and Numba were measured in the same table.
status_note: Actively developed (devel commits through 2026-08-03, PyPI 2.2.3 from 2026-03-20, 398 stars, JOSS 2023 paper) and MIT-licensed. The headline speedups come from the unreleased devel branch and are first-party, so expect the 2.2.3 release figures (about 210x C, 383x Fortran geomean on these kernels) unless you install from git.
